body.text: In just under two weeks, the APEC summit will convene in Shenzhen, where U.S. President Donald Trump has floated the idea of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. However, in the lead-up to the leaders’ meeting, the United States is sending Pyongyang two different messages

The first signal comes from Trump himself. In August he scaled back major military drills with South Korea at the last minute, stressing his “very good relationship” with Kim. He later said that Kim had answered his overtures. Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader’s sister, denied any communication between Trump and Kim Jong Un, but called the personal relationship “still excellent.”

On October 31, Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated that Trump is “open” to a meeting with Kim, although “nothing has been scheduled.” He added that the president “doesn’t view meeting with someone as a concession.”

But the rest of the government seems to be working from a different playbook. Also on October 31, the FBI blamed North Korea for the $6.3 billion Binance theft, the largest crypto heist on record. And just two days before reiterating Trump’s interest in a summit with Kim, Rubio and his South Korean and Japanese counterparts reaffirmed their “resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea during a meeting on the sidelines of a G20 ministerial. Pyongyang has repeatedly said that its nuclear program is no longer up for negotiation.

On November 4, Kim Yo Jong responded to these developments in a press statement, saying that “the continued hostile signal of the U.S. to our state compels the DPRK to reconsider the U.S. entity in various aspects.” (DPRK is an abbreviation for North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.) She specifically objected to the FBI accusation over the Binance hack, the trilateral demand for denuclearization, joint military drills, continued U.S. and multilateral sanctions, and the State Department “Trafficking in Persons Report,” which criticized North Korea. Kim cited these as evidence of “Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward the DPRK.”

A Korean analyst quoted by Reuters read the statement as a reminder that an end to Washington’s “hostile policy” is now a precondition for North Korea to engage in talks. Kim Yo Jong indeed rejected the idea of a meeting under these circumstances. “It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons who refuse to abandon their policy of confrontation while talking about dialogue,” she said in the statement. “…To the hostile signals that the United States continuously sends, we do not know how to respond otherwise.”
Hours later the South Korean military reported another missile launch by Pyongyang, the fourth in a month.

It’s important to note that, of the things Kim directly complained about, only one has seen the U.S. president’s direct involvement – the joint military drills, which Trump dramatically scaled back. The others – the FBI statement on Binance, the State Department report, and allied coordination – reflect the routine operation of U.S. government agencies. In North Korea’s view, this confirms the existence of the U.S. government’s “hostile” policy toward North Korea, regardless of what Trump himself might say.

That is exactly the lesson Kim Jong Un took from the failed Hanoi summit with Trump. As a recent Korea JoongAng Daily column recalled, Kim went to Vietnam in 2019 offering to dismantle the Yongbyon complex in exchange for relief from sanctions affecting civilian economic activity. Trump asked for more, and then-National Security Adviser John Bolton, by his own account, helped derail the deal. Kim returned home empty-handed and punished the officials who had handled the talks. Kim is not keen to undergo a similar embarrassment at a future summit.

Beijing and Moscow aren’t likely to help nudge Kim toward diplomacy. China might be willing to host a Kim-Trump summit, but U.S. experts doubt it will put much effort toward making one happen. Sydney Seiler, a former U.S. intelligence officer for North Korea, told Yonhap News that he does not expect Chinese leader Xi Jinping to take the kind of “political risk” former South Korean President Moon Jae-in did. Victor Cha put it more bluntly, saying China is “really not interested in doing any of the heavy lifting.” China’s leverage partly rests on being the go-between. A direct Trump-Kim deal could erode that advantage.

Kim’s brief trip to the border city of Dandong in late October, where he met senior Chinese official Wang Huning and not Xi, set off speculation about possible coordination before the APEC summit. South Korea’s foreign minister said North Korea-U.S. dialogue may have come up, while other analysts urged caution.

Russia has its own calculus. Kim has contributed troops and weapons for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. In return, Russia provides economic and military cooperation that helps blunt U.N. sanctions. South Korea’s central bank credited economic cooperation with Russia for much of the North’s growth in 2025, according to AFP.

I could find no recent public Kremlin statement on a Trump-Kim meeting, which suggests Moscow sees little to gain from either blocking it or brokering it. Instead, Putin is busy courting Trump directly. The Wall Street Journal reported that he proposed a three-way summit with Trump and Xi to discuss Ukraine after Trump waived key sanctions on Moscow. More recently, Rubio confirmed that Trump will meet both leaders bilaterally around the APEC and G20 gatherings. My reading is that both of Kim’s patrons are negotiating with Trump over bigger files than North Korea.

Kim might have reasons to meet Trump, but Pyongyang wants assurances that denuclearization stays off the agenda. Whatever Trump says, the routine statements coming out of the State Department have called that into question. Trump could try to wall off the Binance accusation and continuing sanctions from leader-level diplomacy, but Pyongyang has shown it will not accept that separation. North Korea is in no hurry to show up for an agenda-less meeting that would amount to any empty photo-op. To secure a summit with Kim, Trump could push the State Department to drop its denuclearization language, which would please Pyongyang. However, that would unsettle Seoul and Tokyo, given that all three just reiterated that common priority.

If a meeting does happen in Shenzhen, it will tell us less about Kim, whose positions are well known, than about Washington. Can the White House and the State Department finally get on the same page – and which one will that be?
